          hot flame extinction and the tests were terminated, which unknowingly and sadly
          shortened the duration of the cool flame combustion.

            In later testing with the long/near thermocouple, two of the tests exhibited repeated
          hot  flame  quenching and  reignition, which  resulting from  intervening  low-
          temperature combustion.   It is likely that the closest thermocouple, approximately 1
       cm from the burner surface, was a factor in the reignition.  The exposed type-B
         thermocouple includes platinum, a catalyst for the oxidation of hydrocarbons. The
            catalysis contributed to the rapid reignition limiting the duration of the low-
          temperature combustion in these tests.

        A challenge for cool flame detection was concern about potential damage to the CFI
            intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter,
          while the intensifier gain is set high.

       When at a small fraction (e.g., less than 10%) of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow
           Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during CFI-G testing, i.e.,
         where actual flow rate differed from that desired.

         Meanwhile, at high flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, the burner does not produce
           spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the
           flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically,
          the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of
          the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical
          burner.  In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At
            sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can
         appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally
         quenches near the supply tube.

          During Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) testing on 23 Dec. 2020, it was discovered that
          the lowest of the 14-micron silicon carbide fibers on the Thin Filament Pyrometry
           (TFP) fiber array had broken. Recovery plans were developed and enacted on 18 Jan.
         2021 to remove the broken fragments from the harp-like array. Unfortunately, the
          next fiber was broken during the delicate operations where the fibers are only spaced
         5 mm apart.  Although ACME does have alternate arrays, it also had months of
          remaining testing, so the decision was made to continue testing with only 3 fibers
           (instead of 5) for the final BRE testing and the subsequent CLD Flame and CFI-G tests.
           This was a minor loss, where the fiber array was only occasionally used in CFI-G
            testing.

     I.  Completeness/Quality of Data
      The experiment’s proposal to CASIS and NSF stated:
                  “It is assumed here that approximately 50 ISS flames can be conducted.
            These will include approximately 12 chamber fills following evacuation.”
       Far more testing was carried out for this experiment, where that included the ignition of
      280 hot flames in 23 days of ISS testing, some of which included multiple chamber fills.
      Although some of the flames were short lived, the testing far exceeded the quantity that
      had been proposed.

      The cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead)
       over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, they are a
       degradation of the image quality.

          It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there
          is not obvious indication of this; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available
      measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).

      Recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is done because of
       operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed per test day.
      Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some image data to
       allow additional tests to be conducted.  This is intentionally done to maximize the
        scientific return of each day of testing within the project constraints.

    J.  Status of Data Analysis
       [provided by the U. of Maryland investigator team and lightly edited by Stocker]
      Data sets of spherical diffusion flames as a function of the fuel mass flow rate (for normal
       flames), the oxidizer mass flow rate (for inverse flames), O2 concentration, fuel dilution,
      and pressure were obtained for all the normal and inverse flame test days. The raw test
      measurements made from devices  - such as thermocouples, photomultiplier tubes
       (PMTs), gas flow meters, and radiometers - were saved in a csv file format per each test.
      The data rate of the non-imaging measurements was 125 per sec.

      The raw data was processed to transform  it into  scientific measurements.  The
      transformed data were visualized as plots for further analysis.  In addition, test images
      recorded in tiff and hobj formats respectively for the CFI intensified camera and ACME
      DataCam have been analyzed to investigate the presence of cool flames and to find flame
       diameters. Of these the intensified camera is of most value, and all of its images to date
      have been converted to video files and reviewed. Since the intensified camera images
      were taken under the maximum possible gain applied, the images were averaged and
        filtered to decrease the overall noise level, and the intensity of the images was increased
      by a factor of 50 to facilitate the search of intensity peaks.

Appendix F. ISS Operations per the Payload Weekly Science Summary

2021 (for all of CFI-G)
First round (normal flames)
Increment 64
Week 21: March 5-11
On GMT 062, the final test points were performed for ACME CLD Flame (Coflow Laminar Diffusion). The
Principal Investigator, Marshall Long from Yale University, considers the experiment to have been very
successful. On this day, 11 flames were ignited, which contributed to the over 300 that were ignited for
all of CLD Flame. Early results show that the dilution limits are extended in microgravity compared to
normal gravity. Steady microgravity flames are also more stable and have lower lift-off heights due to the
lack of buoyancy. We have gathered a superior set of experimental data to be used for improving our
ability to computationally model highly diluted flames. This capability could be implemented in design
tools resulting in more efficient and less polluting combustion here on Earth.

On GMT 068 & 069, Kate Rubins configured the ACME Chamber Insert to support the next ACME
experiment, CFI-G Part 1 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). CFI-G will study flames with unusually
low temperatures known as cool flames. These flames were discovered in 2012 with the first subrack
payload to use CIR, but this investigation only used liquid fuels. ACME’s hardware will allow CFI-G to study
gaseous fuels to gain valuable insight into the combustion processes in engines.

The time-lapse CLD Flame image associated with this submission is not included in this report.

Week 22: March 12-18
On GMT 075, Mike Hopkins lubricated the CIR GC Argon QDs and replaced the gas bottles at CIR Manifold
#2 and CIR Manifold #4. These tasks prepared the CIR for supporting the next ACME experiment, CFI-G
Part 1 (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). CFI-G will study flames with unusually low temperatures
known as cool flames. These flames were discovered in 2012 with the first subrack payload to use CIR, but
this investigation only used liquid fuels. ACME’s hardware will allow CFI-G to study gaseous fuels to gain
valuable insight into the combustion processes in engines.

Week 24: March 26 – April 1
On GMT 088, the first test points were performed for ACME CFI-G Part 1 (Cool Flames Investigation with

        This clip from a test point video shows a 50% butane flame ignited in a chamber atmosphere with
       elevated oxygen at 0.5 atm. The flame is bright and sooty, where the soot is formed when the fuel
       molecules within the flame combine in the absence of oxygen, which is outside the flame. The
       flame is like a bubble that separates the two reactants. The flame shell, like the film of the bubble,

       are trapped in the flame as a temperature gradient drives them away from the flame shell and
       toward the cooler burner. These opposing forces cause some soot clusters to just “dance” in
        place.

       any soot remained when the flame extinguished.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022)                                           21 November 2022


CFI-G studies flames with unusually low temperatures known as cool flames, which were discovered in
2012 with droplet combustion research being conducted in CIR at the time. That experiment burned liquid
fuel droplets, which shrink as they burn. Instead, CFI-G will burn gaseous fuel ejected from a porous
spherical burner to investigate cool flames under quasi-steady conditions. Cool flame chemistry  is
important to ignition, and the results could lead to cleaner burning and more efficient internal combustion
engines.





                         Figure 1. CFI-G Hot Flame of Nitrogen-Diluted Butane

Figure 1 shows a hot flame of nitrogen-diluted butane in an atmosphere of elevated oxygen. The porous
spherical burner of sintered stainless-steel sits on top of the tube that supplies the gaseous fuel. The blue
flame shell is spherical, which is only possible in microgravity without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s
gravity. Spherical flames greatly simplify experimental analysis by reducing the flame structure to a single
dimension, which allows computational models to focus on the chemistry and transport phenomena
rather than the prediction of the flame shape.

The yellow particles are clusters of soot. Their color is the result of thermal radiation and is indicative of
their temperature. Soot is formed when the fuel molecules within the flame combine in the absence of
oxygen, which is outside the flame. The flame is like a bubble that separates the two reactants. The flame
shell, like the film of the bubble, is a thin sheet where the fuel and oxygen come together and react,
producing heat, light, carbon dioxide, and water vapor.

Due to microgravity, the soot remains in the flame longer and forms clusters. Some of these soot clusters
escape the flame because they are pushed by the outward flow of the fuel from the burner. Others are
trapped in the flame as a temperature gradient drives them away from the flame shell and toward the
cooler burner.

nitrogen-diluted propane fuel at chamber pressures of both 2 and 3 atm. Fifteen hot flames were ignited.

Week 10: June 11-17
On GMT 162, 12 nitrogen-diluted ethane flames were ignited for ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation
with Gases) at ambient pressures. Some tests were performed in atmospheres with 21% oxygen, while
some tests were performed in higher oxygen concentrations of 35-40%. During two tests, the 14-micron
ceramic fibers were translated into the flame to optically measure the flame temperature through a
technique known as Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP). On GMT 165, Mark Vande Hei replaced the gas bottles
at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support continuation of CFI-G test points.





                    Figure 1. Flame Temperature Measurement of CFI-G Hot Flame

Figure 1 shows two images of the same nitrogen-diluted ethane flame. The right-hand image has been
enhanced to show the faint spherical flame. The color of the fibers’ glow in the left-hand image is
indicative of the temperature, where yellow is hotter than orange, which in turn is hotter than red. Using
a camera characterized for quantitative measurements, we can determine a radial temperature
distribution across the flame by analyzing the color variation along the length of a fiber.

The top fiber is outside of the flame. Its glow can be used to determine the temperature near the flame,
where it is obviously cooler despite its proximity. The fibers that pass through the flame are much brighter
except for their centers, which are dimmer and cooler. The flame shell separates the fuel and the oxygen,
where the heat, light, carbon dioxide, and water vapor are created at its surface, so the flame is hottest
at its shell.

Week 11: June 18-24
On GMT 174, we ignited 16 nitrogen-diluted butane flames in the final tests for the first round of ACME
CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases). Cool flames remained elusive, where there has been no clear
evidence of these low-temperature phenomena during this round of testing. In the coming weeks and
months, we will review the data more closely to assess their potential presence. Regardless, we gathered
a wealth of valuable data that will improve our fundamental understanding of soot process and flame
dynamics. Since CFI-G tested with different fuels, these data expand upon the results gained from the
other ACME experiments.

Next week, the ACME Chamber Insert will be configured to support the second and final round of CFI-G
testing. This testing will explore the potential existence of cool flames in an inverse configuration. The
flow direction will be reversed, where a mixture of nitrogen and oxygen will flow from the burner into the
Combustion Chamber, which will be filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel. As a result, the
flames will be inside out, where, as an example, the soot will be formed outside of the flame.

      CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG

        In this test point video, soot that forms at ignition escapes from the flame, especially opposite of
       the burner’s supply tube (toward the left). The escaping soot clusters exacerbate the heat loss
       experienced by the flame and cause it to locally quench, creating a hole in the flame. This hole
        allows for direct mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame,
       thereby enhancing flammability. As a result, the flame reforms, closing the hole, but it opens again
      due to heat loss. This repeated opening and closing of the flame creates a visually dramatic flame
        that swirls around the porous spherical burner.

Second round (inverse flames except for the final test day)
Week 12: June 25 – July 1
Recent data analysis shows evidence of cool flames!

Data from several of the ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) tests on GMT 174 indicate
the presence of cool flames. These tests were performed at a chamber pressure of 2 atm with nitrogen-
diluted butane fuel. Cool flames give off little heat or light and were too faint to be visible real time during
testing. But their presence was revealed by thermal radiation and burner temperature measurements
after the hot flames quenched.

Non-premixed (i.e., fuel and oxidizer are not mixed prior to reacting) cool flames were discovered in 2012
with CIR droplet combustion research using liquid fuels. Now, we’ve achieved non-premixed cool flames
using gaseous fuels! Cool flame chemistry is important to ignition and the results could lead to vehicles
that experience less wear on engine parts, get better gas mileage, and create less pollution.

blocks.text: CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG

In this test point video, soot that forms at ignition escapes from the flame, especially opposite of 
the burner’s supply tube (toward the left). The escaping soot clusters exacerbate the heat loss 
experienced by the flame and cause it to locally quench, creating a hole in the flame. This hole 
allows for direct mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, 
thereby enhancing flammability. As a result, the flame reforms, closing the hole, but it opens again 
due to heat loss. This repeated opening and closing of the flame creates a visually dramatic flame 
that swirls around the porous spherical burner. 
 
Second round (inverse flames except for the final test day)  
Week 12: June 25 – July 1 
Recent data analysis shows evidence of cool flames!  
 
Data from several of the ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) tests on GMT 174 indicate 
the presence of cool flames. These tests were performed at a chamber pressure of 2 atm with nitrogen-
diluted butane fuel. Cool flames give off little heat or light and were too faint to be visible real time during 
testing. But their presence was revealed by thermal radiation and burner temperature measurements 
after the hot flames quenched. 
 
Non-premixed (i.e., fuel and oxidizer are not mixed prior to reacting) cool flames were discovered in 2012 
with CIR droplet combustion research using liquid fuels. Now, we’ve achieved non-premixed cool flames 
using gaseous fuels! Cool flame chemistry is important to ignition and the results could lead to vehicles 
that experience less wear on engine parts, get better gas mileage, and create less pollution.

these tests, an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner into the Combustion Chamber filled with
an ethane/nitrogen mixture. We observed that flames in 12% ethane burned longer than those in 6%
ethane. Tests were performed at a chamber pressure of both 1 and 2 atm, and some tests used the array

          Figure 1. Composite Image of CFI-G Inverse Flames at Increasing Oxidizer Flow Rates

Figure 1 compares the flames from three tests with different flow rates of oxidizer from the burner. The
flame size is dependent on the limiting reactant, which for inverse flames is the oxygen.

The porous spherical burner and its supply tube are visible within each spherical flame. Heat loss to the
supply tube causes the flame to locally quench and creates an opening. This opening leads to direct mixing
of the reactants, which would otherwise be separated by the flame shell. Mixing enhances the combustion
and brightens the flame at the opening.

This composite image compares inverse flames with multiples of oxygen/nitrogen flow rates from the

trio of tests.

These flames are locally quenched by heat loss to the burner’s supply tube leaving an opening in the flame.
The opening, which allows reactant mixing, often oscillates in size while growing until the flame fully
extinguishes. In some tests the extinction occurs abruptly, but in others the oscillations can last for tens
of seconds. Meanwhile, some flames are quasi-steady despite the opening. This is one example of how
these spherical flames are not as simple as had earlier been imagined.

                            Figure 1. Example CFI-G Inverse Butane Flame

This example image can be readily identified as an inverse flame because the soot is outside, rather than
inside, of the flame. The soot is formed when the fuel combines with itself at high temperatures in the
absence of oxygen. In this regard, the inverse flame is like a bubble separating the outer fuel from the
inner oxygen, where the two reactants are consumed producing light, heat, and chemical products (e.g.,
carbon dioxide and water vapor). Flames of hydrocarbon fuels are naturally blue, while the high-
temperature soot glows red, orange, yellow, or even white depending on its temperature.

At ignition, this flame was all bright and sooty, but the system is not fully symmetric. There is some
asymmetry to the burner flow, and there is heat loss to the tube supplying the gas to the porous spherical
burner. As a result, the soot faded from the lower hemisphere, which in this image appears to be soot
free. Meanwhile, the upper hemisphere remained enveloped in a layer of glowing soot. Tests like this
have yielded valuable data for improving our understanding of how to control soot generation.

Figure 1. Example CFI-G Inverse Butane Flame 
 
This example image can be readily identified as an inverse flame because the soot is outside, rather than 
inside, of the flame. The soot is formed when the fuel combines with itself at high temperatures in the 
absence of oxygen. In this regard, the inverse flame is like a bubble separating the outer fuel from the 
inner oxygen, where the two reactants are consumed producing light, heat, and chemical products (e.g., 
carbon dioxide and water vapor). Flames of hydrocarbon fuels are naturally blue, while the high-
temperature soot glows red, orange, yellow, or even white depending on its temperature. 
 
At ignition, this flame was all bright and sooty, but the system is not fully symmetric. There is some 
asymmetry to the burner flow, and there is heat loss to the tube supplying the gas to the porous spherical 
burner. As a result, the soot faded from the lower hemisphere, which in this image appears to be soot 
free. Meanwhile, the upper hemisphere remained enveloped in a layer of glowing soot. Tests like this 
have yielded valuable data for improving our understanding of how to control soot generation.

Increment 66
Week 1: Oct. 15-21
On GMT 291, we performed the last 12 tests for ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) during
an extra day of testing with normal flames. The purpose of this extra day was to recreate the test
conditions in which we achieved cool flames in earlier testing, and we successfully achieved cool flames!
In two tests, the butane hot flames extinguished due to radiative heat loss, but then seconds later they
reignited. This extinction and reignition occurred several times during each of these tests. The butane
reignited because a cool flame occurred between the hot flames. Cool flame chemistry is important for
ignition in internal combustion engines and an improved understanding would aid the development of
vehicles that experience less wear on engine parts, get better gas mileage, and create less pollution.

      CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG
        This video clip is from the end of a test in which the hot butane flame repeatedly extinguishes and
         reignites. While the low-temperature cool flames between the hot flames aren’t visible in this
        video, they cause the closest thermocouple to warm enough to visibly glow prior to reignition.

        Reignition causes the temperature to abruptly increase, but then it drops while the hot flame
       burns and weakens. When the hot flame extinguishes and transitions to a cool flame, the
       temperature starts increasing again  until another temperature spike caused by the next
         reignition.

        In another test, we saw evidence of a cool flame where the temperature temporarily rose after
       the hot flame extinguished but not enough to reignite a hot flame.

Week of April 26, 2021
Observing flames
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) include six independent studies of
flames that seek to improve fuel efficiency and reduce pollution from combustion on Earth and help
prevent fires in spacecraft. ACME investigations are conducted in the space station’s Combustion
Integrated Rack (CIR), which includes a combustion chamber, gas bottles, and five cameras for observing
flames. The research aimed at spacecraft fire prevention examines different materials, including how to
put them out when burning, conditions needed for a material to continue burning, and the effectiveness
of existing methods to screen and select materials for spacecraft. The crew replaced controllers for ACME
during the week.

Week of October 11, 2021
Coolest flames in space
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project is a set of six independent studies
of gaseous flames conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The researchers’ goals are to gain
information that can lead to improved fuel efficiency, reduced pollutant production in practical
combustion on Earth, and improved spacecraft fire prevention. One of the ACME studies currently being
conducted is known as the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases. A cool flame is one that burns at about
600 degrees Celsius. A candle is about two times hotter, burning at around 1,400 degrees Celsius. The
results of this investigation could lead to cleaner, more efficient internal combustion engines. This past
week, a crew member was tasked with replacing a butane bottle in preparation for the experiment.

Chamber was re-Inserted into the chamber, and the crew replaced three ACME controllers. The ACME 
project is a set of six independent studies of gaseous flames to be conducted in the Combustion Integrated 
Rack (CIR). ACME’s primary and secondary goals are (1) improve fuel efficiency and reduce pollutant 
production in practical combustion on Earth, and (2) spacecraft fire prevention through innovative 
research focused on materials flammability. 
 
2021 Oct. 13: GMT 286 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR):  A crewmember replace the CIR Manifold #2 Bottle with a new bottle 
containing 40% O2 and 60% N2.  The Manifold #4 Bottle was also replaced with a new bottle containing 
30% C3H8 and 70% N2. These bottle changes are in preparation of continued Cool Flame experiment 
runs.  The CIR includes an optics bench, combustion chamber, fuel, and oxidizer control, and five different 
cameras for performing combustion investigations in microgravity. 
 
2021 Oct. 14: GMT 287 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR):  A crewmember replaced the CIR Manifold #4 Bottle with a new bottle 
containing 30% C4H10 and 70% N2. The CIR includes an optics bench, combustion chamber, fuel and 
oxidizer control, and five different cameras for performing combustion investigations in microgravity.

Appendix M. Summary of the ISS data collection
The CFI-G data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other
ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were
subsequently transported to the ground.

The CFI-G image data includes images from the following cameras:
    1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but
       those settings were consistent within each individual test)
    2.  CFI intensified camera, used always (or at least nearly so) with a formaldehyde filter for CFI-G
    3.  High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the
       opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off
The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and
HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format.  In contrast, the analog video was
recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format.

The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D).

The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through
NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

   N.3 Awards
    In 2021, CFI-G Principal Investigator Peter Sunderland was inducted as a Fellow of the Combustion
    Institute for his “significant contributions to understanding laminar flame dynamics and soot
    formation and oxidation.”

   While the awards proceed the CFI-G experiment, CFI-G Co-Investigator Forman Williams was
    recognized by the Combustion Institute with the Silver Combustion Medal (1978) and the Bernard
    Lewis Gold Medal (in 1990). He furthermore was induced in the inaugural 2018 class of Fellows of the
   Combustion Institute for his “pioneering investigations in energy and combustion including nitric
    oxide emissions, spray and turbulent combustion, chemical kinetics and fire research.”

   N.4 Outreach
   NASA   Project   Scientist  Dennis   Stocker  created  the  Space  Flames  Facebook  page
    (www.facebook.com/space.flames) and Flickr site (https://www.flickr.com/photos/space-flames),
   where some entries are specific to CFI-G. He continues to administer these sites, where most content
    thus far has been about the ACME project of which CFI-G is a part. As an example of educational
    outreach, a simple board game related to the ACME’s spherical flames experiments can be
   downloaded   from   https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/space/iss-research/iss-fcf/cir/acme/downloads/.

   be downloaded from that page. Printed copies of fact sheets have been distributed at meetings of

   Meanwhile, NASA promoted awareness of ISS combustion research with the video ‘The Power of
    Studying Combustion on the ISS’ which was posted on March 13, 2018.

   Awareness of ISS combustion research, including the ACME project, was promoted on Oct. 15, 2018
   by The Combustion Institute in their online news article, “International Space Station (ISS) Combustion
    Experiments.”

   A photo collage and 1-paragraph article on ACME by Michael Greshko titled “Cosmic Combustion”
   was published on page 22 of the Oct. 2022 issue of the National Geographic Magazine, for which there
     is an online version. While general to ACME, the article addresses CFI-G with a statement about the
    flames: “In microgravity they can swell into ethereal … orbs that can burn at a surprisingly cool 900
    degrees Fahrenheit (a gas stove burner’s high setting  is about 3100oF).”  Despite  its brevity,
    Sunderland and Stocker were both interviewed for the article.

    Stocker is involved in a broad range of NASA educational outreach to students and teachers, Scouts
    of both genders, and the general public.  His primary outreach focus  is the fundamentals of
    microgravity and human spaceflight, for example through microgravity design challenges which he
    helps create and administer. But he periodically addresses other topics, e.g., where he sometimes
    speaks on ‘NASA and the Science of Superman’ – for example at the Superman Celebration in
    Metropolis, IL.  In this regard, his NASA outreach is carried out locally, regionally, nationally, and
    online.  For example, he regularly presents on microgravity at Space Center Houston’s Space
    Exploration Educators Conference (SEEC). He has exhibited the last five National Scout Jamborees,
    five national Boy Scout conferences, the last three national Girl Scout conventions, and the 2019
   World Scout Jamboree (which was held in the U.S.). Stocker has been a key lead for the agency in
   NASA’s participation in these Scouting events, where as an example the latter outreach is visually
    described at www.nasa.gov/feature/stem/world-scout-jamboree.html.

NASA’s participation in these Scouting events, where as an example the latter outreach is visually 
described at www.nasa.gov/feature/stem/world-scout-jamboree.html.

Figure 1. Preliminary False-Colored Image of Hot Ethane Flame for CFI-G This false-colored image shows a spherical flame, which is only possible in microgravity without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity. Spherical flames greatly simplify experimental analysis by reducing the flame structure to a single dimension, which allows computational models to focus on chemical kinetics and transport phenomena. The hot flame in Figure 1 has a hole at the bottom because of heat loss to the fuel tube, which supplies the ethane to the porous sphere. The three bright lines passing through the flame are 14-micron ceramic fibers, which were translated into the flame to determine temperature measur

Figure 1. CFI-G Hot Flame of Nitrogen-Diluted Butane Figure 1 shows a hot flame of nitrogen-diluted butane in an atmosphere of elevated oxygen. The porous spherical burner of sintered stainless-steel sits on top of the tube that supplies the gaseous fuel. The blue flame shell is spherical, which is only possible in microgravity without the buoyant flows created by Earth’s gravity. Spherical flames greatly simplify experimental analysis by reducing the flame structure to a single dimension, which allows computational models to focus on the chemistry and transport phenomena rather than the prediction of the flame shape. The yellow particles are clusters of soot. Their color is the result of th

Figure 1. CFI-G Hot Flame of Nitrogen-Diluted Propane Figure 1 shows images of a CFI-G hot flame from two different cameras. The left image is from a color camera. The right image, which has been false-colored, is from an intensified camera filtered for formaldehyde (CH2O) emissions, which are associated with cool flame chemistry. When cool flames were first discovered in 1809, Sir Humphrey Davy observed a “pale phosphorescent light.” Residual soot created during ignition escapes from opposite sides of the flame. In the right image, soot is visible as light spots, such as at the top of the porous sphere. Week 6: May 14-20 On GMT 137, ACME CFI-G (Cool Flames Investigation with Gases) test poi

Figure 1. False-colored Image of a CFI-G Flame with Residual Soot Clusters Figure 1 shows a hot flame of nitrogen-diluted ethane in an atmosphere with elevated oxygen and pressure. Initially, the flame was bright yellow with soot, and over time some of the soot escaped from the flame. This preliminary false-colored image is from later in the test, where residual soot clusters were still visible within the flame when it self-extinguished due to excessive heat loss. Week 9: June 4-10 On GMT 159, Shane Kimbrough replaced the gas bottle at CIR Manifold #2 to support continuation of CFI- G test points.

Figure 1. Flame Temperature Measurement of CFI-G Hot Flame Figure 1 shows two images of the same nitrogen-diluted ethane flame. The right-hand image has been enhanced to show the faint spherical flame. The color of the fibers’ glow in the left-hand image is indicative of the temperature, where yellow is hotter than orange, which in turn is hotter than red. Using a camera characterized for quantitative measurements, we can determine a radial temperature distribution across the flame by analyzing the color variation along the length of a fiber. The top fiber is outside of the flame. Its glow can be used to determine the temperature near the flame, where it is obviously cooler despite its proxi

Figure 1. Composite Image of CFI-G Inverse Flames at Increasing Oxidizer Flow Rates Figure 1 compares the flames from three tests with different flow rates of oxidizer from the burner. The flame size is dependent on the limiting reactant, which for inverse flames is the oxygen. The porous spherical burner and its supply tube are visible within each spherical flame. Heat loss to the supply tube causes the flame to locally quench and creates an opening. This opening leads to direct mixing of the reactants, which would otherwise be separated by the flame shell. Mixing enhances the combustion and brightens the flame at the opening. Week 17: July 30 – Aug. 5 On GMT 209 and 216, we ignited 23 inve

Composite Image of CFI-G Inverse Flames at Increasing Flow Rates This composite image compares inverse flames with multiples of oxygen/nitrogen flow rates from the porous spherical burner faintly seen within the flames. The oxygen flows outward until it reaches sufficient fuel to be consumed. As such, the tests with the greater oxidizer flow rates result in larger flames. Radiative heat loss scales with flame size, and the larger flames are dimmer than the smaller flames. The oxygen/nitrogen ratio, propane concentration, and Combustion Chamber pressure were consistent in this trio of tests. These flames are locally quenched by heat loss to the burner’s supply tube leaving an openin

Figure 1. CFI-G Inverse Flames at Increasing Oxidizer Flow Rate and Butane Concentrations This composite image shows the effects of both the oxidizer flow rate from the burner and the butane concentration on the inverse flames. The oxygen concentration was held constant in these four tests. From bottom to top, the oxidizer flow rate was doubled, which greatly impacted the flame size. From left to right, the ~20% increase in the butane concentration had a more subtle effect. At the higher fuel concentration, the flames are slightly smaller and much brighter. Week 24: Sept. 17-23 Megan McArthur replaced the gas bottle at CIR Manifold #2 on GMT 263 and the gas bottle at CIR Manifold #4 on GMT 2

Figure 1. Effects of Butane Concentration on a CFI-G Inverse Flame Figure 1 is a graph of the thermal radiation emitted by an inverse flame, and it compares two tests with the same oxidizer mixture ratio and flow rate but a different butane concentration. The dim flame in the 14.0% butane experienced large oscillations (shown in blue on the graph) due to heat loss to the burner’s supply tube. These oscillations grew in strength until the flame self-extinguished. In contrast, the flame in 17.5% butane was much brighter. It eventually experienced similar oscillations (shown in red on the graph), but they were weaker and didn’t cause the flame to extinguish during the test. Week 26: Oct. 1-7 On

Figure 1. Example CFI-G Inverse Butane Flame This example image can be readily identified as an inverse flame because the soot is outside, rather than inside, of the flame. The soot is formed when the fuel combines with itself at high temperatures in the absence of oxygen. In this regard, the inverse flame is like a bubble separating the outer fuel from the inner oxygen, where the two reactants are consumed producing light, heat, and chemical products (e.g., carbon dioxide and water vapor).
